Fulfilling a customer's order › Stage 2: Accept the order

Runbook: Accept the order draft, generated from the register

New to this stage?
The stage on one page how a case moves through it, its outcomes, what is at stake

An online store selling outdoor clothing and equipment to signed-in customers through a web front end (and a mobile app), with orders accepted, stock-checked, paid and shipped by back-end services joined by a message broker. Configuration described: the Aspire AppHost as deployed to Azure Container Apps, with UseFoundry=true so the chat and embedding models are present; Postgres, RabbitMQ and Redis run as the application's own containers. proposed: no source says which configuration runs in production; this is the fullest the repository defines. In this configuration the services run outside Development, so /health is not mapped and logs default to Information.

StepRight outcomeFrom → toDone byNeeds
Step 2.1: The order is released for stock checking when the grace period ends(proposed) AwaitingValidation within 1.5 minutes of "OrderDate", with its OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidation outbox row at State 2 (Published)Submitted → AwaitingValidationOrder Processor, Ordering APIOrdering database, Event bus
Step 2.2: Stock is confirmed for every item of the order(proposed) StockConfirmed only when every ordered product is in the catalogue with AvailableStock of at least its units; Description 'All the items were confirmed with available stock.'AwaitingValidation → StockConfirmedOrdering API, Catalog APIOrdering database, Catalog database, Event bus
Other outcome: The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock(proposed) Cancelled, with Description naming the products without stockAwaitingValidation → CancelledOrdering API, Catalog APIOrdering database, Catalog database, Event bus
Expected outcome: Payment is taken for the order(proposed) Paid, with the order total taken once from the buyer's payment methodStockConfirmed → PaidOrdering API, Payment ProcessorOrdering database, Event bus
Other outcome: The order is cancelled because payment failed(proposed) Cancelled, with no payment takenStockConfirmed → CancelledOrdering API, Payment ProcessorOrdering database, Event bus
Other outcome: The order is cancelled at the customer's request(proposed) Cancelled before any payment is takenSubmitted → Cancelled; AwaitingValidation → Cancelled; StockConfirmed → CancelledClientApp, Mobile BFF, Ordering APIOrdering database, Identity API

Expected of the stage. A case that enters it leaves within the promise (proposed: 2 minutes from entering Submitted, read from the timing of “The order is released for stock checking when the grace period ends”, “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order” and “Payment is taken for the order”: a 1-minute grace period and up to 30 seconds to the next poll, then 10 seconds before StockConfirmed and 10 before Paid. The stage is entered when the record is created, so a case's age in it is now minus "OrderDate"), in one of these ways:

  • Other outcome: The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock: (proposed) Cancelled, with Description naming the products without stock
  • Expected outcome: Payment is taken for the order: (proposed) Paid, with the order total taken once from the buyer's payment method
  • Other outcome: The order is cancelled because payment failed: (proposed) Cancelled, with no payment taken
  • Other outcome: The order is cancelled at the customer's request: (proposed) Cancelled before any payment is taken

What is at stake.

  • Order id ("Id"): The only key that joins the order across services and to the customer
  • Order total (sum of Units x UnitPrice): Money the customer pays; value blocked while the order is stuck
  • Items and units (ordering."orderItems"): What must be in stock and shipped
  • Buyer (ordering.buyers "IdentityGuid"): Who is waiting and who is told
  • Delivery address: Where the goods must arrive
  • Payment method (card number masked to the last four digits): What is charged
  • Cannot be undone: Payment is taken for the order
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is released for stock checking when the grace period ends” fails: counted in orders held in Submitted past the grace period. Every poll publishes again for orders still Submitted
  • Customer experience and trust, if “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order” fails: counted in orders stranded in AwaitingValidation. A lost or failed message is not sent again; nothing polls AwaitingValidation
  • Customer experience and trust, if “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order” fails: counted in orders confirmed with an item the catalogue does not hold. The check skips a product it cannot find, so the order is confirmed
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock” fails: counted in orders stranded in AwaitingValidation after their stock was rejected. Same mechanism as step 2.2
  • Customer experience and trust, if “Payment is taken for the order” fails: counted in orders stranded in StockConfirmed, not paid. A lost payment request or result is not sent again
  • Money directly at stake, if “Payment is taken for the order” fails: counted in order totals not collected for orders stranded in StockConfirmed. Value blocked: the order total is not taken while the order waits
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is cancelled because payment failed” fails: counted in orders stranded in StockConfirmed after a failed payment. Same mechanism as the expected outcome “Payment is taken for the order”
  • Customer experience and trust, if “The order is cancelled at the customer's request” fails: counted in cancel requests that fail, so the order goes ahead. The customer gets an error and must try again. A cancel that lands while payment is in flight leaves the order Cancelled and the payment result ignored; with a real gateway that would be money taken for a cancelled order

Is Ordering database down or unreachable?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering databaseReads Ordering database accepting connections
How to check
In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run pg_isready -d orderingdb
Not the cause if accepting connections
The cause if no response, or rejecting connections
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: action 7
Why this check reads it this way
The ordering database does not answer: Ordering API's status change fails and the answer is acknowledged and gone; the shared postgres server also takes catalogdb down

Is Event bus down or unreachable?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Event busReads Broker running
How to check
In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmq-diagnostics -q ping
Not the cause if Ping succeeded
The cause if no answer
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: action 7
Why this check reads it this way
The broker does not answer: Ordering API's post-commit publish is marked failed (the check “Are Ordering API's outbox rows marked failed?”), Catalog API's too (the check “Are Catalog API's outbox rows marked failed?”), and Payment Processor's result is lost (the check “Is Payment Processor failing to publish its messages?”). Messages already queued wait only if the broker keeps its data: the AppHost gives it no data volume

Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?

Not the cause if well below max_connections

Is Ordering database slow?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering databaseReads Long-running statements on orderingdb
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb, then:

SELECT count(*) FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE datname = 'orderingdb' AND state = 'active' AND now() - query_start > interval '5 seconds';
Not the cause if 0
The cause if 1 or more, persisting
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering database
Why this check reads it this way
Statements run long: the poll, the status writes and the outbox writes finish late, and orders leave late. A statement that fails outright shows as the unavailable rows instead (the same fault for the moves after Submitted)

Is Event bus slow?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Event busReads Broker resource alarms and headroom
How to check
In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmq-diagnostics check_local_alarms; and memory and disk free against their watermarks in rabbitmqctl status
Not the cause if no alarms, memory and disk well inside their limits
The cause if no alarm yet, but memory or disk close to its watermark
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Event bus
Why this check reads it this way
The broker slows publishing connections when its queues cannot keep up; memory or disk nearing its watermark is a leading sign of the alarm in the check “Is Event bus full or out of capacity?”. Messages arrive late and the orders move late (the same fault for the moves after Submitted)

Is Event bus full or out of capacity?

Not the cause if no alarms

Is Order Processor not polling?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by statePart Order ProcessorReads Grace-period releases published; Order Processor exits and restarts
How to check

Read the last 300 lines of order-processor's console log (az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for lines 'Publishing integration event:', and its system log for exits:

az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type system
Not the cause if A 'Publishing integration event:' line every 30 seconds for each Submitted order past 1 minute; no exits
The cause if No such lines, and the container exited or is not running
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: action 1
Why this check reads it this way
Order Processor is not running, or its background service has ended: an exception from a publish is not caught in the poll loop, and.NET's default for a failed background service is to stop the host. No order leaves Submitted

Is Ordering API not running, leaving its messages queued?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering APIReads Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers
How to check
In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers, and read the row for queue Ordering
Not the cause if consumers 1 or more
The cause if consumers 0, with messages waiting
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: action 5
Why this check reads it this way
Ordering API's consumer is not attached: the service is down, or its bus start returned without consuming because the connection was not open or setup failed, and nothing retries it. Messages wait in the durable queue Ordering as persistent messages and are handled when it returns

Is Order Processor's poll query failing?

How to check
Search the console log of order-processor (az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error querying confirmed grace period orders after grace period'
Not the cause if No such line

‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state

Is Order Processor polling but missing cases?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by statePart Order ProcessorReads Grace period and poll interval in effect
How to check
Read BackgroundTaskOptions__GracePeriodTime and BackgroundTaskOptions__CheckUpdateTime in order-processor's configuration (az containerapp show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg>), else the shipped appsettings.json
Not the cause if 1 and 30 (the shipped values)
The cause if A different value, larger than the age of the held orders allows
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: action 3
Why this check reads it this way
The poll selects by its own settings: GracePeriodTime in minutes and CheckUpdateTime in seconds. A changed or mis-entered value (seconds written as minutes) holds orders in Submitted while the poller runs and logs normally

Is Order Processor failing to publish its messages?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by statePart Order ProcessorReads Event bus start failures; Grace-period releases published
How to check
Search the console log of order-processor (az containerapp logs show --name order-processor --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Error starting RabbitMQ connection' at its last start, and for the service ending just after a 'Publishing integration event:' line
Not the cause if Neither
The cause if Either one
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: action 4
Why this check reads it this way
The publish of GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent throws. The configured retry does not retry it, because Execute runs an async lambda. The exception escapes the poll loop and ends the service, as in the check “Is Order Processor not polling?” (Polly's Execute overloads: https://www.pollydocs.org/api/Polly.ResiliencePipeline.html: an async lambda binds to Execute<TResult>(Func<TResult>), so the pipeline only sees the returned task)

Are the messages for Event bus accepted but routed to no queue?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by statePart Event busReads Bindings on exchange eshop_event_bus
How to check
In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_bindings source_name destination_name routing_key, and read the rows whose source is eshop_event_bus
Not the cause if eshop_event_bus Ordering GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent is listed
The cause if That binding is missing
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state
Ending Yes → Restore: action 5
Why this check reads it this way
GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent reaches queue Ordering only through a binding Ordering API makes at its start. It is published mandatory but nothing handles returned messages, so without the binding it is dropped. The next poll publishes again

Is Ordering API failing on the messages it reads?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by statePart Ordering APIReads Ordering API messages it failed to handle; Ordering API messages of an event type it does not know
How to check
Search the console log of ordering-api (az containerapp logs show --name ordering-api --resource-group <rg> --type console --tail 300 --format text (one replica per call; add --replica for the others)) for 'Unable to resolve event type for event name GracePeriodConfirmedIntegrationEvent', or 'Error Processing message' with no 'Error Handling transaction for' line beside it whose quoted message body carries the OrderId of an order still Submitted (the line quotes the body but names no event: EventBusRabbitMQ/RabbitMQEventBus.cs:172)
Not the cause if Neither
The cause if Either, repeating every 30 seconds
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state
Ending Yes → Can’t restore here: escalate to the owner of Ordering API
Why this check reads it this way
The message cannot be read: an unknown event name is logged and dropped, and a body that does not deserialize throws; either way the message is acknowledged and gone. The order stays Submitted and the next poll sends it again

Is Ordering API falling behind on its queue?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering APIReads Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers
How to check
In the eventbus container (az containerapp exec --name eventbus --resource-group <rg>) run rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages consumers, and read the row for queue Ordering, twice, a minute apart
Not the cause if messages near 0 and not growing
The cause if messages growing while consumers is 1 or more
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: action 6
Why this check reads it this way
Ordering API handles its queue on one consumer, one message at a time, and the stock answers and the payment-succeeded answer each wait 10 seconds first. Above about six such answers a minute per instance the queue grows; every 30 seconds the poll adds another release message for each order still Submitted, feeding it

Not the cause if No such line

Setting AwaitingValidation and writing its outbox row run in one transaction; if it throws, it rolls back, the order stays Submitted, and the message is acknowledged and dropped. The next poll sends it again

Are changes in Ordering API left unpublished in its outbox?

Used by Orders past the acceptance promise, by state, Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failedPart Ordering APIReads Ordering outbox rows not published, by State
How to check

In the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb, then:

SELECT o."Id", o."OrderStatus", l."State", l."EventId" FROM ordering.orders o LEFT JOIN ordering."IntegrationEventLog" l ON (l."Content"::jsonb ->> 'OrderId')::int = o."Id" AND ((o."OrderStatus" = 'AwaitingValidation' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToAwaitingValidationIntegrationEvent') OR (o."OrderStatus" = 'StockConfirmed' AND l."EventTypeName" LIKE '%OrderStatusChangedToStockConfirmedIntegrationEvent')) WHERE o."OrderStatus" IN ('AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - o."OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes';
Not the cause if "State" 2 (Published) on every row
The cause if "State" 0 (NotPublished) or 1 (InProgress)
‹ Back to Orders past the acceptance promise, by state ‹ Back to Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
Ending Yes → Restore: action 7
Why this check reads it this way
The status and its outbox row commit together, and the row is published only by the same request right after the commit. A crash or lost connection in between leaves it at State 0, or 1 if it died mid-publish, and nothing sends it later

Orders paid with no money moving are counted by “Orders marked paid with no payment taken”
Causes the design rules out, so no check is needed
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: the move writes only the new status and an outbox row built from the order's own items, and acts only from Submitted
  • Ordering API, relay not running: there is no relay process; the request that commits the status publishes its rows itself. What it leaves behind is the check “Are changes in Ordering API left unpublished in its outbox?” and the check “Are Ordering API's outbox rows marked failed?”
  • Catalog API, relay not running: no relay; the handler publishes its own row at once
  • Catalog API, the act completes wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A product the catalogue does not hold is skipped and the order confirmed, and a stock check reserves nothing: wrong, but the order moves on. Counted by “Orders confirmed with an unknown item” at step 2.2
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the promise. The stock and payment setters act only from their expected state and otherwise change nothing, and a cancellation of an order already Cancelled sets it Cancelled again, so a late or repeated answer leaves the order out of the stage or where another move put it
  • Payment Processor, the act fails: the decision reads one setting and nothing before the publish can throw; a publish failure is the check “Is Payment Processor failing to publish its messages?”
  • Ordering API, callee down: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Ordering API down, so Mobile BFF cannot reach it
  • Mobile BFF, callee down: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Mobile BFF down, so the app cannot reach it
  • Ordering API, callee returns an error: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Ordering API answers 500 'Cancel order failed to process.'
  • Ordering API, callee slow or hangs: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the cancel is slow; the main path is not waiting on it
  • ClientApp, caller gives up mid-call: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the app gives up; if Ordering API finished the cancel, the order is Cancelled and leaves the stage
  • Ordering API, the act fails: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the cancel command throws or returns false; a throw is caught by the identified-command wrapper, which returns false, so Ordering API reports the cancel failed with 500 'Cancel order failed to process.'
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: a cancellation that lands while the release or the stock check is in flight leaves the order Cancelled, and the late message is ignored because each setter acts only from its expected state
  • Ordering API, the act completes wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A cancellation while payment is in flight leaves the order Cancelled and the payment result ignored: wrong, and with a real gateway money taken for a cancelled order, but the order is out of the stage. Counted by “Orders cancelled while their payment went ahead”
  • Ordering database, unavailable: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the ordering database for the cancel write; the same fault on the main path is the check “Is Ordering database down or unreachable?” to the check “Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?” and the check “Is Ordering database down or unreachable?” to the check “Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?”
  • Ordering database, slow: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the ordering database for the cancel write; the same fault on the main path is the check “Is Ordering database down or unreachable?” to the check “Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?” and the check “Is Ordering database down or unreachable?” to the check “Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?”
  • Ordering database, full or out of capacity: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: the ordering database for the cancel write; the same fault on the main path is the check “Is Ordering database down or unreachable?” to the check “Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?” and the check “Is Ordering database down or unreachable?” to the check “Is Ordering database full or out of capacity?”
  • Identity API, unavailable: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Identity API, whose keys Ordering API uses to check the customer's token; the main path carries no token
  • Identity API, slow: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Identity API, whose keys Ordering API uses to check the customer's token; the main path carries no token
  • Identity API, full or out of capacity: as a cause of orders held past the promise. A failed cancellation leaves the order on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancel request fails. Counted by “Cancel requests refused or failed” at the other outcome “The order is cancelled at the customer's request”. Here: Identity API, whose keys Ordering API uses to check the customer's token; the main path carries no token
  • Ordering API, callee answers wrongly: as a cause of orders held past the promise or cancelled by a failure. The cancel call's answer is the result of the order's own cancel command: Ordering API answers 500 'Cancel order failed to process.' when the command fails, and OK when it succeeded or when its request id was seen before, even on a first attempt that failed. Either way the order stays on the main path, which moves it on by itself; the cancellation's own outcome is “Ordering API, the act completes wrongly”
  • Ordering database, answers stale or wrong: the ordering database is one postgres server with no replica or cache in front of it, so every read sees the last committed write
  • Catalog database, answers stale or wrong: the catalog database is a database on the same single postgres server, with no replica or cache in front of it
  • Event bus, answers stale or wrong: the broker carries the messages and answers no read a move decides on; a message lost, unrouted or late is tested by the message modes
  • Identity API, answers stale or wrong: as a cause of orders held past the promise or cancelled by a failure. Ordering API requires the shopper's token on the cancel call, which Identity API issues; a stale or wrong answer from it fails the cancellation, which leaves the order on the main path, as in “Identity API, unavailable”

What not to do.

  • Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  • Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  • Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists
  • Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed: the poll selects only Submitted
  • Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first

Declare an incident when the operators’ severity definition says to: the register holds no trigger for it. What is at stake here, for that call, is under The stage on one page. Keep working the entry while it is declared.

What to hand over: the alert and what it guards (its entry); the affected case ids by state; whether new cases are still affected now; which checks ran and what they showed; what was contained and what was done; the look-back time.

Close
EndingClose
Already knownLink the incident, then close.
Planned changeLink the window or change, then close. Note that the alert should have been suppressed, if it should.
Self-healedOnly for an alert that counts cases waiting: confirm it is back under its threshold, then close. Note that its threshold or window may be wrong.
RestoreAfter the action, confirm the alert is under its threshold, no case it counted is still affected, and new cases get through. Any that remain: back to its entry.
Can’t restore hereEscalate, and hand over.
None of the checks explains itEscalate with what you have, and note the gap in this runbook.
None of the checks explains it

For the cases no check explained: escalate them with what you have, and note the gap in this runbook (a cause it does not cover, or a check that could not be run). Then go on with the next group of cases that still has some: an unexplained group does not end the walk for the others.

Before you start: the access you need

You need to be able to read each of these. A check you cannot run is a gap in this runbook: note it.

  • Order Processor: Grace-period releases published; Order Processor exits and restarts; Grace-period poll query failures; Grace period and poll interval in effect; Event bus start failures
  • Event bus: Bindings on exchange eshop_event_bus; Broker running; Broker resource alarms and headroom
  • Ordering API: Queue Ordering: messages waiting and consumers; Ordering API messages it failed to handle; Ordering API messages of an event type it does not know; Ordering API transaction failures, by command; Ordering outbox rows not published, by State; Ordering API publish failures
  • Ordering database: Ordering database accepting connections; Long-running statements on orderingdb; Connections to the postgres server against max_connections
  • Catalog API: Catalog outbox rows by State; Catalog API publish failures; Queue Catalog: messages waiting and consumers; Catalog API messages it failed to handle
  • Payment Processor: Payment Processor messages it failed to handle; Payment results published, by kind; Queue PaymentProcessor: messages waiting and consumers
  • Order: Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed
  • Catalog database: Catalog database accepting connections; Long-running statements on catalogdb; Connections to the postgres server from catalogdb
  • Deployment, configuration and restart history for Order Processor, Ordering API, Catalog API, Payment Processor, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Identity API.

Runbook: Accept the order › Alert

Orders past the acceptance promise, by state

An order still in Submitted, AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed past the promise has not been accepted when the shopper expects, and the moves out of AwaitingValidation and StockConfirmed strand it with nothing to move it again (lifecycle “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”, “The order is cancelled because an item is out of stock”, “Payment is taken for the order” and “The order is cancelled because payment failed”, recovery stranded)

It has been above the operators’ threshold for longer than their window (the alert).

Its cases those held in the stage past the bound. A case not past the bound is not one of this alert's.
Look back from when the oldest of its cases entered the stage, to now. The alert fires only once a case has waited past the bound, so its cause can be as old as that: never read a test over only the time since the count began rising.
Do now
  1. List its cases and set the look-back. Every check below runs on these cases, over that time. List them with the alert’s own count:
    How
    SELECT "OrderStatus", count(*) FROM ordering.orders WHERE "OrderStatus" IN ('Submitted','AwaitingValidation','StockConfirmed') AND now() - "OrderDate" > interval '2 minutes' GROUP BY 1 (the interval is the stage's proposed promise); in the postgres container (az containerapp exec --name postgres --resource-group <rg>) run psql -U postgres -d orderingdb
  2. Contain. No hold is needed: the cases the alert counts are still in the stage, and nothing more is done to them while they wait.
  3. Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  4. Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  5. Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists
  6. Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed: the poll selects only Submitted
  7. Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first
  8. Escalate or declare as soon as a trigger is met, at any point below. Triggers ›
Check first
1Is this already known?
How
Look for an open incident, or a known error with a fix in flight, for any of these parts: Order Processor, Ordering API, Ordering database, Event bus, Catalog API, Catalog database, Payment Processor, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Identity API. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if one is open: link it and close.
Yes → Already known
2Was it planned?
How
Look for a maintenance window on any of those parts, or a planned change to a timing the stage depends on (Grace period GracePeriodTime 1 minute, polled every CheckUpdateTime 30 seconds. Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted. The bus's retry policy never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set. Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, queued behind the other waits as in “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”). Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a window is open or a setting was changed on purpose: link it and close.
Yes → Planned change
3Did something change when it started?
How
Look for any deploy, configuration change or unplanned restart of those parts since the look-back time above. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a change lines up with the start.
Yes → Roll the change back, or escalate to the owner of the part that changed
4Is it already recovering?
How
Read the alert's own count over one window (for a count of cases waiting, with the oldest only just past the bound). Not the cause if it is not falling; it is recovering if the count falls within one window: confirm it is back under its threshold, then close.
Yes → Self-healed
Find the cause in order, on its cases only. No → next check. Yes → take its ending for the cases it lists, and go on for the rest. A check whose evidence lists no cases (a match in a log or a metric) explains no case by itself: note it, if the match falls inside the look-back, and go on; a case no later check explains takes the ending of every check noted for it, each named in the hand-over; where those endings differ, escalate rather than restore. A result you cannot read, or a check you cannot run: note it for the hand-over and go on. Where a command asks for a time span in angle brackets, give it the look-back above; where it asks for case ids in angle brackets, give it the ids of the cases you are working.
Group its cases by the state they are in (Submitted, AwaitingValidation, StockConfirmed) and work each group below that has cases, the largest first.

Runbook: Accept the order › Alert

Orders cancelled in acceptance because payment failed

A payment outage cancels every order that reaches StockConfirmed (“The order is cancelled because payment failed”), and none of them waits, so “Orders past the acceptance promise, by state” stays flat while the shopper loses the order

It has been above the operators’ threshold for longer than their window (the alert).

Its cases those that left by “The order is cancelled because payment failed” from StockConfirmed in the alert's window. A case still in the stage is not one of this alert's.
Look back from when the earliest of its cases entered the stage, to now: what sent a case out wrongly can come before it left.
Do now
  1. List its cases and set the look-back. Every check below runs on these cases, over that time. List them with the alert’s own count:
    How
    ordering-api log lines 'Handling integration event:' naming OrderPaymentFailedIntegrationEvent, one per order, searched over the window in the log store, against the orders that entered acceptance in it ("OrderDate" in ordering.orders)
  2. Contain. Stop more cases leaving by “The order is cancelled because payment failed”: no person makes these moves, so nothing here holds more cases back; they keep leaving until the cause is restored.
  3. Do not set "OrderStatus" straight to 'StockConfirmed', 'Paid' or 'Cancelled' by SQL: the events are raised only inside the setters, so no outbox row is written and nothing after it happens (payment, stock reduction, notifications)
  4. Do not set an outbox row's "State" back to 0 to have it sent: nothing reads unsent rows after the request that wrote them
  5. Do not look for failed messages to replay: a consumer acknowledges a message it failed on, and no dead-letter queue exists
  6. Do not restart order-processor to move orders held in AwaitingValidation or StockConfirmed: the poll selects only Submitted
  7. Do not restart the postgres or eventbus container apps as a first move: no data volume is declared for either, so find out where their data lives first
  8. Escalate or declare as soon as a trigger is met, at any point below. Triggers ›
Check first
1Is this already known?
How
Look for an open incident, or a known error with a fix in flight, for any of these parts: Order Processor, Ordering API, Ordering database, Event bus, Catalog API, Catalog database, Payment Processor, ClientApp, Mobile BFF, Identity API. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if one is open: link it and close.
Yes → Already known
2Was it planned?
How
Look for a maintenance window on any of those parts, or a planned change to a timing the stage depends on (Grace period GracePeriodTime 1 minute, polled every CheckUpdateTime 30 seconds. Every run re-publishes for each order still Submitted. The bus's retry policy never retries a failed publish: Execute is given an async lambda, so the failure lands in the returned task, not the call; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set. Ordering API consumes its queue with one consumer on one channel, so these waits queue behind one another; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, queued behind the other waits as in “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”; 10 seconds of simulated work before the status is set, on the same single consumer as “Stock is confirmed for every item of the order”). Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a window is open or a setting was changed on purpose: link it and close.
Yes → Planned change
3Did something change when it started?
How
Look for any deploy, configuration change or unplanned restart of those parts since the look-back time above. Not the cause if there is none; the cause if a change lines up with the start.
Yes → Roll the change back, or escalate to the owner of the part that changed
4Is it already recovering?
How
Read the alert's own count over one window. Not the cause if it is not falling; a falling count means only that no new cases are arriving, and the cases it counted stay wrong: this check never closes the alert, so go on and work them.
Yes → No new cases: go on and work the ones it counted
Find the cause in order, on its cases only. No → next check. Yes → take its ending for the cases it lists, and go on for the rest. A check whose evidence lists no cases (a match in a log or a metric) explains no case by itself: note it, if the match falls inside the look-back, and go on; a case no later check explains takes the ending of every check noted for it, each named in the hand-over; where those endings differ, escalate rather than restore. A result you cannot read, or a check you cannot run: note it for the hand-over and go on. Where a command asks for a time span in angle brackets, give it the look-back above; where it asks for case ids in angle brackets, give it the ids of the cases you are working.
